title: Compare and Contrast Network Topologies, Architectures, and Types

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: A network topology describes how systems and devices are arranged and communicate. Architecture identifies functional layers, while north-south and east-west describe traffic direction.
bullets: Mesh, hybrid, star/hub and spoke, spine and leaf, and point to point
sections.callout: How is it connected? → How is it organized? → Which way is traffic moving?

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When CompTIA describes device connections or traffic movement, can you identify the topology, architecture, or flow?
bullets: Center with branches → Star/hub and spoke
Exactly two endpoints → Point to point
Core and distribution combined → Collapsed core
Into or out of an environment → North-south

entries.title: Mesh
paragraphs: Mesh provides multiple interconnections and alternate paths. A full mesh connects every participating node to every other node; a partial mesh provides redundancy without every possible link.
entries.recognitionCue: The design emphasizes redundant interconnections → Mesh.

entries.title: Hybrid
paragraphs: A hybrid topology combines multiple topology designs in different parts of the network.
entries.recognitionCue: The network combines star and mesh characteristics → Hybrid.

entries.title: Star/Hub and Spoke
paragraphs: A central point connects endpoints or remote sites. A LAN switch can be the center of a star; headquarters can be the hub for WAN branches. The hub can become a central dependency unless redundant.
entries.memoryHook: Every road leads to the center.
entries.recognitionCue: Branches connect through headquarters → Hub and spoke.

entries.title: Point to Point
paragraphs: A point-to-point link directly connects exactly two endpoints, such as routers or locations.
entries.recognitionCue: Two endpoints have a dedicated direct link → Point to point.

sections.title: Spine and Leaf
paragraphs: Spine-and-leaf is a modern data-center architecture. Leaf switches connect endpoints and resources; spine switches provide high-speed connectivity among leaves. A typical design connects each leaf to each spine, producing predictable redundant paths for east-west traffic.
sections.callout: Data center + many server-to-server flows → Spine and leaf.

sections.title: Three-Tier Hierarchical Model

entries.title: Access
paragraphs: The access layer connects endpoints such as PCs, phones, printers, and wireless APs.

entries.title: Distribution
paragraphs: The distribution layer aggregates access connectivity and commonly applies routing and policy.

entries.title: Core
paragraphs: The core layer provides fast backbone connectivity among major network areas.

sections.callout: Access → Distribution → Core = enter → organize → move fast.

sections.title: Collapsed Core
paragraphs: A collapsed-core architecture combines the distribution and core functions into one tier, with a separate access tier. It simplifies networks that do not require three distinct layers.

entries.title: North-South
paragraphs: North-south traffic moves into or out of an environment, such as a user accessing the Internet or an Internet client reaching a hosted application.

entries.title: East-West
paragraphs: East-west traffic moves laterally within an environment, such as application-server-to-database-server or VM-to-VM traffic.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Central hub and branches → Star/hub and spoke

entries.title: Mesh vs. Hub and Spoke
paragraphs: Mesh provides interconnected alternate paths. Hub and spoke depends on a central location.

entries.title: Three-Tier vs. Collapsed Core
paragraphs: Three-tier separates core and distribution. Collapsed core combines them.

entries.title: Spine and Leaf vs. Three-Tier
paragraphs: Spine and leaf is a data-center fabric; three-tier is an access/distribution/core hierarchy.

entries.title: North-South vs. East-West
paragraphs: North-south crosses the environment boundary. East-west stays within the environment.
